content.text: Callers are traced. The main candidate is the new variable-bounding code in `shell_parse.py`, which can hide aliases. Writing up the findings now.

findings.explanation:
_bound_values runs over every entry in ctx.variables. That includes the internal security-state keys: ALIAS+name, FUNCTION+name, HASHED+name, NAMEREF, READONLY and DESCRIPTOR, not just user variables. New values are put at the front (shell_state `(*items, *invalid, *earlier)` and shell_model `(*values, *earlier)`), so the cap drops the OLDEST possible values. Dropping them silently removes definitions that may still be in force.

There are two ways to exploit this:
(1) Run `alias ls='git reset --hard'` (or `X=git`), then add 64 conditional redefinitions like `false && alias ls=echo1; ...`. The dangerous definition is dropped. `ls` (or `"$X" reset --hard`) is then analysed only against harmless alternatives.
(2) Build a value of more than 1 MiB with a few doublings (`P=a; P=$P$P` x21), then `alias ls="git push -f origin main;#$P"`. The single value is too large, so `kept` is empty and ALIAS+ls is deleted. That is the same state as 'no alias', and `ls` is parsed as plain ls (`_expand_alias` returns the words unchanged when the key is missing).

The only signal is `ctx.result.truncated = True`. The rm_rf_guard rule has a regex fallback for rm, but the dangerous_commands rules (git reset/push -f, sql-destructive, fetch-and-execute, chmod, etc.) do not deny on truncation. bash_risk_judge only acts on it when JEV is enabled. Deleting a value or alias therefore turns 'possibly dangerous' into 'unknown/benign', and the check fails open.
findings.fix: Fail closed when bounding values. Do not drop or delete internal keys (ALIAS/FUNCTION/HASHED/NAMEREF/READONLY/DESCRIPTOR/positionals); for them, record an 'unknown' marker that makes the command word dynamic and denies or asks. For user variables, replace the dropped values with a marker that makes later expansions dynamic, not a smaller known set. Also make dangerous_commands treat `parsed.truncated` as ask/deny (or run a raw-text fallback scan) instead of trusting the incomplete parse.

findings.explanation: _forces now treats any `o` in a short-option cluster as the start of the `-o <push-option>` value and ignores every letter after it. This is only correct for `git push`, and only when `o` is actually the option letter. Check every command whose `_forces` result gates a deny: for a git subcommand where `o` is a flag with no value, `-of` / `-xof` now hides the force flag. Even for push, a cluster such as `-vof` treats `f` as the value of -o, which matches git. A wrapper or another subcommand reaching `_forces` (line 305) where `o` takes no value would be a bypass.
findings.fix: Apply the `-o<value>` split only when the subcommand is `push` (where -o/--push-option takes an argument). Otherwise keep the old check, `"f" in arg[1:]`.
